gen-silkscreen-gf-murecho: Retro and a little lo-fi, Silkscreen spaces its letters out so you can almost feel the gaps. Murecho then takes over with wide-open s curves, a modern plain sans that gives the pixel look room to breathe.
gen-silkscreen-gf-noto-sans-cypro-minoan: Silkscreen spaces every letter apart, retro and lo-fi, with strokes that never thin or swell. Noto Sans Cypro Minoan is the sans-serif counterpart, cutting its terminals back to leave a big gap.
gen-silkscreen-gf-noto-sans-linear-b: Modern and lo-fi at once, Silkscreen swaps hairline joins for full-width strokes, each letter spaced like spaghetti laid out. Noto Sans Linear B does smooth curves instead.
gen-silkscreen-gf-noto-sans-mongolian: Silkscreen has a thickness like neon glass tubing, with retro letters spaced so far apart you can almost feel the gaps. Noto Sans Mongolian flares its terminals outward instead.
gen-silkscreen-gf-noto-sans-nko-unjoined: Silkscreen lays its lo-fi letters out like spaghetti, with no brush-style pressure swelling anywhere in the line. Noto Sans NKo Unjoined brings wide openings on small letters.
gen-silkscreen-gf-noto-sans-shavian: Silkscreen keeps a flat, unvarying line weight through every retro letter, each one spaced apart like spaghetti. Noto Sans Shavian follows with rope-loose curves, a plain sans that never knots at its ends.
gen-silkscreen-gf-quattrocento-sans: Retro pixels, spaced out loose. Silkscreen is best at lo-fi display moments, its joins as thick as the stems, while Quattrocento Sans keeps c clearly apart from o for modern, clean text.
gen-silkscreen-gf-roboto-flex: Lo-fi and spaced out, like signage. Silkscreen holds one plain line weight in every letter, but Roboto Flex, a sans-serif with a wide slot in the c, would look oversized if blown up large.
gen-silkscreen-gf-rosario: Retro letters, lots of breathing room. Silkscreen draws its bowls without any thinning at the sides, while Rosario, a plain sans, leaves the ends of its c open and never turning inward.
gen-silkscreen-gf-ruluko: Spaced-out, lo-fi, and retro. Silkscreen makes round letters with walls as heavy as the straight ones, while Ruluko, a sans, does its best work with broad open counters on c and s.
